newsitem.title: USA: Drought, disease seen hurting U.S. spring wheat.
newsitem.headline: Drought, disease seen hurting U.S. spring wheat.

text.p: Participants on one leg of a U.S. spring wheat tour said an early-summer drought and disease caused a significant reduction in the wheat's yield potential.

On the second day of the three-day tour, wheat samples from two durum fields in McLean County produced a calculated average yield potential of 22.1 bushels per acre (bpa). Last year, the county's durum yielded 25.8 bpa, and the county's five-year average is 33.2 bpa, according to USDA.
"We are seeing a lot of shorter, smaller heads, fewer spikelets per head and fewer kernels per spikelet," said Jim Peterson, North Dakota Wheat Commission marketing specialist.
Peterson said an early summer drought in North Dakota had caused head sizes to be smaller than in previous years.

Members on this leg of the tour sampled a dark northern spring wheat field in Ward County, in north central North Dakota, calculated an average yield potential of 19 bpa. That compares with that county's actual 1996 yield of 32.3 bpa and the five-year average of 33.2.
Participants on this leg of the tour said the sampled fields were typical of durum and spring wheat fields in that area.
Last year, this same tour route calculated on the second day a spring wheat yield potentional of 33.0 bpa and durum yield potential 30.0 bpa.
"The surprising thing is, we are seeing leaf disease like tan spot and septoria," said Peterson. "Especially when you had dry conditions, to see the disease on top of thinner stands is surprising."

Approximately 55 farm group, grain company and government representatives and journalists were participating in this year's tour and participants will issue a final average yield potential when it concludes Thursday afternoon in Fargo.
